text: Yes. Yes, I’ve been trying to raise the alarm about this for a decade, and I’m relieved that people are finally listening. I think that AI could bring some great benefits if we navigate it well, but if we navigate it poorly then it really does risk killing every human on the planet. I feel like we’re kind of trapped in a race here, where we at Anthropic think we can do it more safely than our other competitors, both domestic and abroad. But it’s an insane race, because we’re taking on an incredible amount of risk. We’re taking on far, far more risk than NASA takes on for a crewed shuttle flight, except instead of risking seven volunteers, we’re risking the entirety of humanity. The risk is far too high. I would desperately prefer that the whole race be slowed internationally so that we could approach this problem more carefully, and get the benefits with far fewer risks. But right now the world is not set up that way, and so I think it’s better for Anthropic to be in the lead. I’m hopeful that this event is the moment where the message finally breaks through, so that the whole world can notice the danger and coordinate to slow down. However, the abstract and distant nature of long-term risks makes them hard to approach from a policy perspective: our view is that it may be best to approach them indirectly by addressing more imminent risks that serve as practice for them. [T]here will be powerful models; they will be agentic; we’re getting towards them. If such a model wanted to wreak havoc and destroy humanity or whatever I think we have basically no ability to stop it. So8res Nov 19, 2026 182 11 30 Share Anthropic is making its initial public offering tomorrow, so this seems like a fine day to discuss how Anthropic is utterly failing to live up to their responsibilities. Leaders of AI companies regularly acknowledge a sizable chance that superintelligent machines would destroy humanity. Their excuse for pursuing it anyway is that while they can’t stop the train , they can race more safely than the competition . 1 Is it moral to build a technology that threatens everyone’s life, if you think you can do the job safer than the competition? Does it change the moral equation if you get paid billions of dollars along the way? I don’t have a confident answer about what the right thing to do is under these dire circumstances. But I am confident of this: if you wish to take the responsibility of building superintelligence onto your own shoulders, it comes with an even greater responsibility to do everything in your power to change the circumstances. Is Anthropic doing everything in its power to stop the AI race? I don’t think so. I think they’ve done more to downplay the dangers than they’ve done to stop this reckless race. You might protest that Dario has been very clear about his views that AI could be dangerous; that he writes about it on his blog and talks about it sometimes on the news. Let’s take a look at how he talks about it on the news, shall we? When asked by Anderson Cooper in September, “Do you earnestly believe that AI could kill all humans?”, Dario changed the topic to insisting that Jacob Coxon (who had recently resigned) wasn’t primarily expressing concerns about Dario’s organization (a claim disavowed by Coxon almost immediately). The closest Dario comes to answering Anderson’s question is to claim that the “chance that things go wrong” is “not all that high”, which seems to fly in the face of Dario’s statements elsewhere . Or consider his conversation with Jo Ling Kent , also in September. When she asked “OK, so we’re here to talk about the concern that AI really could kill us all in the not so distant future. What’s the risk of this actually happening?” he switched the topic immediately to talking about the benefits, with only abstract acknowledgement that there could be risks if the technology was built the wrong way. When Kent pushed back, asking “Do you think the government fundamentally understands what’s possible here?”, he switched to talking about how Coxon wasn’t really criticizing Anthropic, per se, and then added that “We are talking to the government every day. [...] I’m optimistic that if we keep working together with them, we can update them on the latest.” These interviews happened in the wake of Coxon’s resignation. It was a moment where the mainstream media was, finally and at long last, noticing that AI poses a real bona-fide extinction threat. These major mainstream reporters were representatives of the public, asking point-blank for clarity. And Dario basically told them “it’s okay; we have it handled; go back to sleep.” Imagine that, when Anderson Cooper asked “Do you earnestly believe that AI could kill all humans?”, Dario answered: Yes. Imagine the effect that those answers would have had on the world. Now go back and watch those clips again. Contrast Dario’s statements with the statements above. I won’t say that he was lying; I think he was saying sentences he believed. But I do think he was dissembling . The American public was making its first fumbling efforts towards figuring out what the fuck is going on with AI, and Dario was out there vibing “this is all fine; you don’t have to worry about it too much; we’ve got this under control.” I consider this sort of response from someone who joined the AI race to be beyond the pale. I know a lot of people who think that Dario’s actually doing a pretty good job of talking about the dangers. He’s analogized AI to a country worth of geniuses in a datacenter! He’s analogized it to a Tsunami! He’s called for the “pacing” of the frontier! I acknowledge that. But it reads to me like a dogwhistle for AI researchers who are going to be grumpy if he says nothing, while downplaying the dangers as much as possible otherwise. This is clearer if you contrast what he says to congress with what he says to podcasters. Here’s Dario’s testimony to congress on existential risks: However, the abstract and distant nature of long-term risks makes them hard to approach from a policy perspective: our view is that it may be best to approach them indirectly by addressing more imminent risks that serve as practice for them. This was about three years ago. Maybe he thought that the risks were long-term and distant in 2023? Nope! Fourteen days later, he told the podcaster Dwarkesh that the risk might be as little as 2-3 years away, adding: [T]here will be powerful models; they will be agentic; we’re getting towards them. If such a model wanted to wreak havoc and destroy humanity or whatever I think we have basically no ability to stop it. Just look at the sheer difference between Dario’s statements intended for a technical audience and the statements intended for congress. 2 When he speaks to congress, he dissembles. I’m picking on Dario here because it’s the day of Anthropic’s IPO, but the public statements from Sam Altman and Demis Hassabis have if anything been even worse . 3 And even they are doing better than the CEOs who don’t seem to understand or acknowledge the dangers at all. Regardless, let’s step back from the specifics. This is not what it would look like if the companies were actually trying to stop the reckless race. AI companies are not leaping at every opportunity to warn the world that we face an imminent extinction threat. They use those opportunities to emphasize the benefits, talk only abstractly about the dangers, and suggest that maybe the solution is that there should be an embedded evaluator like in a bank, all while implying that we shouldn’t really worry our little heads. They are not lobbying for the international coordination it would take to stop the AI race globally, and buy time for humanity to figure out how to navigate these dangers. On the contrary, they’re lobbying for weak self-serving regulation that would make it even harder for judges to stop them. They are not trying to coordinate with other labs to stop the AI race domestically, hiding behind the excuse that antitrust law prohibits this. This is despite (1) common sense interpretation of the law that companies are allowed to coordinate for a non-commercial reason of averting the literal apocalypse; (2) assurances via White House Accords that they are cleared to coordinate in this way; and (3) their extraordinarily well-resourced legal team. Major AI labs did not hesitate for a second to push the boundaries of AI copyright law when the laws were in the way of training smarter models. So if they start hesitating about murky laws only when it comes time to slow the race, that tells you a thing or two about their real priorities. What would it look like, if they were actually trying? Occasionally, I find myself in conversation with someone in a leadership position at a frontier AI company. Sometimes, when I express that I think they’re shirking their responsibilities, they ask what I think they could do. Here’s a list based on the one I was sending around to the labs this summer (updated lightly in wake of recent events): Improve safety and security practices: Clearly, loudly, and publicly state what would cause you to halt AI R&D. Release as much information to the public as possible, so that there is full transparency about how fast the field is developing, and about how well AI alignment is going. Make detailed, concrete, candid plans for aligning superintelligence and make them public, or make it clear that there is no plan. Run pause/pacing drills . Communicate the danger more loudly and clearly: Create a communications team at your organization that honestly communicates with the public. It should be one of the higher priorities of your organization to have a full-time team clearly stating things like, “The dangers look drastically higher than any engineer would accept on a bridge, or than NASA would accept on a crewed rocket launch. This is really bad, because it threatens all of civilization.” Treat cases like Coxon’s resignation as an opportunity to alert the world to the grave nature of the stakes. Strongly encourage your employees to speak up about their actual views incessantly. Give employees extensive leeway to appear on podcasts to talk about how crazy it is that the world is rolling the dice with all of our lives. If you wouldn’t push a button to cripple a large fraction of the scientific community’s ability to have an honest public discussion here, then don’t push that button for your own employees. Create a prominent website banner warning the public. If you think you’re building machines that threaten the lives of your family and your world, you should be at least as loud and disruptive about this as Wikipedia is willing to be with a routine fundraiser. To do anything less sends a strong signal that you aren’t earnest about any of your talk of risk, that it isn’t truly urgent or worth even minor costs/distractions to your users, that recent AI progress is business-as-usual, etc. Signal boost the worries of your researchers , and make it clear that to a significant extent we’re flying blind and rolling the dice with humanity’s future. If Evan Hubinger or Jan Leike or Paul Christiano or roon are saying things that would shock policymakers to their core, then the CEO should also be saying those exact same things. If the CEO disagrees with the many researchers who think we may be about to lose the future, then he should at least give these views top billing in quotation marks , and say why he disagrees. Make a candid press statement , saying “This is the most dangerous thing humanity has ever done; the world should be going far more slowly; we wish we didn’t have to race, and we feel trapped. An international moratorium is warranted on a timescale of weeks , not years.” Candidly brief Congress in public , begging for an urgent US-China deal to halt the race. Tour other countries to raise an alarm. This should include costly stunts like getting on your knees and begging the UN to do something about the problem urgently, saying this is an ongoing emergency, or other things that break people out of the sense that this is all business as usual. Be loud and candid about the fact that you weren’t being fully candid previously: Acknowledge and apologize for your company’s past pattern of softpedaling the risk, and publicly commit to doing otherwise going forward. When a massive pattern of misleading statements over the years is never acknowledged, it becomes harder to believe that an organization has turned over a new leaf. Provide a long list of the many concrete missteps, such as this one (where the new Anthropic Institute created to “advance the public conversation about AI” said that AI “may also create new challenges, including abrupt economic changes and broad societal impacts”, which is a funny way of acknowledging that leadership thinks AI could extinguish humanity) or this one (where discussion of AI risk was turned into a literal ad for Claude). Emphasize the sharpness of the change , if you can do so honestly. Communicate that you’re coming clean, to the extent that you really are and to the extent that that’s possible. Replacing senior staff who were involved in past communications blunders would be a great way to credibly signal that the change isn’t just rhetoric. Being concrete and loud about the mistakes also helps (e.g., “the situation has gotten a lot more urgent” and/or “now that we’ve see the consequences, we think the old approach was counterproductive”). Do postmortems and root cause analysis and publish those. (See also Nathan Calvin pointing out that Anthropic doesn’t seem to be doing much root cause analysis of how their lobbyists wound up pushing weak, self-serving draft legislation.) Support helpful policy responses: Actively fight against efforts to left-code or polarize this issue. Be willing to lose some important Democratic allies for the sake of building a coalition with both parties. Put a huge amount of funding into things like tamper-proof location verification technology and tamper-proof monitoring technology on advanced AI chips, alongside lobbying for international slowdown. AI companies haven’t done any of this stuff. Wikipedia spends more effort getting you to donate $2 every year than AI companies spend trying to alert the world to the fact that they’re gambling with your life. It might be okay to gamble with everyone’s life if that’s the only way to protect them from the next guy making a worse gamble. But that excuse only works if you’re also trying with all your might to get the whole gamble called off. The AI companies are not living up to that standard. Mealy-mouthed corporate platitudes might even be making the situation worse. “This technology could kill all of you, but I have to make it anyway” sounds hypocritical on its face, so the average person assumes that there must be some sort of ulterior motive: maybe marketing hype, maybe regulatory capture, maybe a liability shield; but the companies aren’t acting like they really actually believe their warnings. I’m sympathetic to the average person here. I think many people at the AI companies believe the dangers are real, but the companies as a whole sure aren’t acting like it. To people inside the AI companies, I’d say: I think you have conversations with your friends and your coworkers that are much more blunt and candid than the communications your company makes to the public. I wish you’d speak your concerns aloud. I wish your communications department would let you. I hope you use your influence inside the company to reorient Anthropic’s entire comms policy. I hope that you use your newfound wealth to take up some of the responsibility that your company has neglected. To everyone else, I’d say: Anthropic is trying to create machines vastly smarter than humans. Their alignment science lead — one of the people responsible for making those AIs good — has said they “do not yet have a plan” and are “not clearly on track” to get one. They’re trying to build machines that are smart enough to replace humanity, and their plan is to figure it out as they go. This is insanely dangerous. Anthropic, and every company like them, must be stopped. If you agree, there’s a rally to ban self-improving AI tomorrow (Nov 19) at 11:00am at the Anthropic offices. If you can’t make it, you can join other protests later , and you can call your congress member to express concern. Anthropic is not trying to stop the AI race with all its might. So we’ll just have to stop it without them. The other reason for racing that the CEOs tend to give is that AI will have a lot of benefits. They are very insistent about reminding people of the benefits. But given that they’re slinging around numbers like 10–25% chance of a civilization-scale catastrophe, “the benefits” are not a sufficient justification for racing ahead. Even if the odds of success really were 80% (which I doubt), it’s fallacious to imagine that our options are limited to “roll those dice” and “lock ourselves into the status quo forever.” We also have the option of slowing down and finding some other path forward that gets us the benefits without risking the life of every last man, woman, and child on the face of the planet! The only possible way to justify a >5% chance of literally ending the world with your own inventions (over the alternative of finding a safer way to do whatever it is you’re doing) is if you’re trying to save the world from an even greater threat. So the argument that “if we don’t do it, the other guys will do it worse” is the linchpin in any justification for racing. There’s almost surely another great gap between his statements intended for a broad technical audience and his statements intended for a narrow one. We have evidence of this. Elon Musk does much better! He just floats around being like “haha yeah there’s no chance we’re gonna control it; we’ve just gotta hope it’s nice to us; there’s a 10–20% chance it’s not; I wish we weren’t doing this so fast.” It’s possible to do! Lightning does not strike you down on the spot. Every other CEO should grow a pair of balls and be more like Elon in this regard. And then Elon should grow a second pair of balls and start trying as hard as he can to stop the fucking race, alongside his efforts to lead the race insofar as it’s going to happen with or without him. Imagine how much the world would change if he personally called Trump and told him the situation was serious and that AI really is likely to kill us all if he doesn’t negotiate a deal with China. Imagine how much more it’d change if he went all-out.
